motd: Type 'help' for the commands, 'man <command>' for one of them.
Your files are in /home/{user}. The rest of the disk is the system's.
New here? Read 'cat ~/start-here.txt', and type 'job' for the one you are on.
help: files     ls cd pwd cat head wc touch mkdir rmdir rm cp mv echo find du
system    uname uptime date ps kill free df dmesg whoami id hostname history
network   iwlist iwconfig dhclient ifconfig ping lodestar (the web browser)
hacking   mmap bruter tdump tnet mbus   (in ~/bin; run on a network you have joined)
job       the contract you are on, and whether it is done (how: ~/start-here.txt)
other     nano sha1sum sleep clear color man help shutdown reboot
Keys: Tab completes, Up/Down history, Ctrl+C stops, Ctrl+L clears, wheel scrolls back.

man.ls:
ls [-l] [-a] [path...]
  List a directory. -l: long form, with owner, size and date. -a: also the hidden (dot) files.
man.cd:
cd [dir]
  Change the working directory. No argument: your home. '..' is the directory above.
man.cat:
cat file...
  Print files. /proc/cpuinfo and /proc/meminfo describe the hardware and its memory now.
man.head:
head [-n N] file
  Print the first N lines of a file (10 by default).
man.wc:
wc file...
  Count lines, words and bytes.
man.touch:
touch file...
  Create empty files, or update their time.
man.rm:
rm [-r] path...
  Remove files; -r also directories with everything in them. There is no undo.
man.cp:
cp src dst
  Copy a file. It is read off the disk and written back, and takes as long as the drive needs.
man.mv:
mv src dst
  Move or rename a file or directory.
man.echo:
echo text [> file | >> file]
  Print text, or write it to a file (> replaces it, >> adds to its end).
man.find:
find [dir] [-name pattern]
  Walk a directory tree and print every path in it (or those whose name matches; * matches anything).
man.du:
du [-s] [path]
  Disk usage of a tree, in KB.
man.uname:
uname [-a]
  The system's name (-a: with the kernel, the host and the machine).
man.uptime:
uptime
  Time since boot, and the load.
man.ps:
ps
  The processes in memory: id, user, resident memory (KB) and name.
man.kill:
kill pid
  Stop a process. Only your own; the system's belong to root.
man.free:
free [-m]
  Memory: total, used by the kernel and the processes, free. A program that does not fit in what is free does not start.
man.df:
df [-h]
  Disk space: size, used, available.
man.dmesg:
dmesg
  The kernel's messages since boot.
man.hostname:
hostname
  This machine's name on the network.
man.history:
history
  The commands typed in this session.
man.lshw:
lshw
  The hardware: processor, memory, disk, network adapters.
man.ifconfig:
ifconfig [iface]
  The network interfaces and their addresses.
man.iwconfig:
iwconfig [wlan0]
  Show the wireless interface. To join a network:
    iwconfig wlan0 essid "NAME" [key KEY]
  An open network needs no key. Then run 'dhclient wlan0' to get an address.
man.sha1sum:
sha1sum file...
  A file's SHA-1 checksum. It reads the whole file: slow on a big one.
man.lodestar:
lodestar [address]
  The web browser, full screen. F6 (or Ctrl+L) types an address, the arrows scroll, Tab/Right and Left pick a link, Enter follows it, Backspace goes back, F5 reloads, Home opens the start page, F10 (or Ctrl+Q) closes it. Needs a network: join one first (iwlist, iwconfig, dhclient).
man.nano:
nano [file]
  Edit a text file, full screen. ^O (or F3) writes it, ^X (or F2) leaves, ^K cuts a line, ^U pastes it, ^G is the help. Only your home and /tmp can be written.
man.acpi:
acpi [-a] [-V]
  The battery: charging or not, its charge and the time left. -a: the AC adapter too. -V: also the battery's wear and the temperature. The adapter is plugged in only where you sit inside a building with power.
man.man:
man command
  The manual page of a command.
man.shutdown:
shutdown
  Halt the system and power off. The next time the lid opens, it boots again.
man.iwlist:
iwlist [wlan0] [scan]
  Scan for the wireless networks in range: their name, channel, signal and whether they are locked.
man.dhclient:
dhclient wlan0
  Ask the network for an address once the card has joined one (see iwconfig). Fails if the key was wrong or the signal is gone.
man.ping:
ping host
  Send packets to a host and time the replies. 'ping gw' pings the router. Needs an address first.
man.mmap:
mmap [ip]
  Map the hosts on the network you have joined: each one that answers, and the services on its open ports. With an address, just that host. Join a network and get an address first (iwconfig, dhclient).
man.bruter:
bruter <ip> [login]
  Try the built-in word list against a host's console (port 23). Prints the password if the login uses a weak one. For consoles you are authorised to test.
man.tdump:
tdump [-c count]
  Capture the frames on the joined network: beacons, probes, the WPA four-way handshake, ARP, DHCP, DNS and TCP. What reads in the clear follows the encryption: an open or WEP network (you hold the key), or a station whose handshake was captured. A technician logged into a utility console leaks the login that way. -c caps the count (default 60).
man.tnet:
tnet <ip>
  Open a console on a host's port 23. It asks for a login and password; once in, 'help' lists what that box does (a substation breaker, a traffic cabinet). 'exit' disconnects.
man.mbus:
mbus <ip> [read | write coil 0 <0|1>]
  Talk modbus/TCP to a device on port 502. 'read' lists its holding registers (an RTU's telemetry: bus voltage, feeder current, frequency, breaker). 'write coil 0 1' closes the breaker, '... 0' trips it. Modbus has no login of its own: reaching 502 is enough. For devices you are authorised to control.

home.start-here.txt:
PRIMER -- read this once.

This notebook runs a plain Unix shell: you type a command, it runs, it
prints. Nothing here reaches the outside until you put the card on a
network yourself.

Looking around
  help            the list of commands
  man <command>   what a command does, and its options
  ls              list a directory      cd <dir>   move into one
  cat <file>      print a file   (this one: cat ~/start-here.txt)
Your files are in /home. The rest of the disk belongs to the system.

The tools in ~/bin came with the notebook, not from any store:
  mmap    the machines on a network you have joined
  tdump   listen to the traffic on it
  bruter  try a word list against a login
  tnet    open a console on a machine
  mbus    talk straight to an industrial controller

The job
A fixer sends work to your phone. Reply YES from the phone to take it.
Type 'job' here to see the one you are on.

The first one wants a place dark for the night. Power comes from a
substation, and each has its own maintenance radio -- a network named
GRIDLINK-nn -- that only appears when you stand next to it.

  1. Walk to the substation, sit, open the notebook (N).
  2. iwlist                  a strong GRIDLINK-nn means you are there.
  3. iwconfig wlan0 essid "GRIDLINK-nn" key <10 digits>
     dhclient                the key is on your phone's Wi-Fi screen.
  4. mmap                    find rtu-nn (the breaker), usually on .10.
  5. trip the breaker, either way:
       mbus <rtu-ip> write coil 0 0       no login, over port 502.
       tnet <rtu-ip>, then: breaker open  needs the operator password.
     for that password: bruter <rtu-ip> operator, or leave tdump
     listening until a technician logs in and reads it off the wire.
  6. The district goes dark; your phone buzzes when you are paid.

The names and numbers change with every network -- read your own
screen, not these. And everything you do is logged where you stand,
so don't linger.
